title: The Coffeehouses That Changed the World
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Coffeehouses That Changed the World.

hook.text: The insurance industry, the stock market, and the French Revolution all started in coffeehouses.

buildup.text: London's 17th-century coffeehouses — called 'penny universities' — charged one penny for coffee and free discussion.

discovery.text: Lloyd's of London started in Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse. The London Stock Exchange began in Jonathan's Coffee House.

twist.text: King Charles II tried to ban coffeehouses in 1675 — calling them hotbeds of sedition. Public outcry reversed the ban.

climax.text: French revolutionaries like Desmoulins rallied support in Café de Foy — coffeehouses fueled political upheaval.

punchline.text: Coffee didn't just wake people up. It woke up entire civilizations.

quiz.question: What famous institution started in a London coffeehouse?

details.summary: European coffeehouses in the 17th and 18th centuries became centers of intellectual exchange, business, and revolution. Lloyd's of London started as a coffeehouse. The London Stock Exchange began in Jonathan's Coffee House. French Revolution plans were hatched in Parisian cafés.
details.whyItMatters: Coffeehouses created the public sphere — spaces where ideas freely circulated regardless of social class. Many modern institutions began as coffeehouse conversations fueled by caffeine rather than alcohol.
takeaways: Lloyd's of London and the Stock Exchange began in coffeehouses
French Revolution plans brewed alongside coffee in Parisian cafés
Coffee replaced beer as the daytime drink, sharpening public discourse

faq.question: Why were coffeehouses called penny universities?
faq.answer: For the price of a penny — the cost of a cup of coffee — anyone could sit and listen to or join conversations with scientists, merchants, and politicians. Coffee houses were democratic intellectual spaces where information flowed freely. The penny admission leveled social barriers.

faq.question: How did coffee change European intellectual life?
faq.answer: Before coffeehouses, public gathering places were taverns where alcohol impaired thought. Coffee sharpened minds instead. The switch from depressant to stimulant as the social drink coincided with the Enlightenment, the Scientific Revolution, and the rise of modern business institutions.
